106.title: Instruments in the room
106.hook: harmonium and tabla today, and older strings like the rebab and saranda
106.howItsDone: Gurdwara kirtan today is often sung with harmonium and tabla, while a growing number of musicians and schools also teach the older string instruments, such as the rebab, saranda, taus and dilruba.

segments.voice: Yesterday, raag, the musical mood of every hymn. Your line was music carries meaning. Did one song's mood reach you before its words? Day one hundred six.

During kirtan in a gurdwara, look toward the front, near the Guru Granth Sahib. Often a few musicians sit on a low platform. One or two have a small wooden box in front of them, pumping a bellows at the back with one hand and pressing keys with the other. Another sits behind a pair of drums, fingers flickering. It all looks ancient and timeless. But in Guru Nanak's gatherings, as Sikhs tell it, none of those instruments were there. There was a man with a stringed instrument across his lap. The sounds in the room have changed. What they're for hasn't.
screen: `THREE MUSICIANS AT THE FRONT.` → `A BOX, A BELLOWS, TWO DRUMS.` → `NOT WHAT NANAK HEARD.`

segments.voice: Start with the box. That's the harmonium, a small reed organ. Punjabis often just call it the vaaja. It came to India with Europeans in the nineteenth century, and a hand-pumped version made for sitting on the floor caught on fast. Today it's at the heart of gurdwara kirtan. Beside it, the tabla, a pair of hand drums, keeping the rhythm and the pulse. Now go back further. Guru Nanak's companion Mardana played the rebab, a plucked string instrument, and you met him on day thirty-one. Tradition links other string instruments to later Gurus: the saranda, a bowed instrument, to Guru Arjan; the taus, shaped like a peacock, to Guru Hargobind; the dilruba to Guru Gobind Singh. Before the tabla, the older drum was the jori, a pair played with the hands. In recent years, Sikh musicians and schools have been bringing these string instruments back. Some say the harmonium's fixed notes can't bend the way a raag wants to, and the old strings suit gurbani better. Others love the harmonium, because it's easy to learn and carries a congregation well, and it's how their grandparents sang. Both are heard in gurdwaras today, often side by side. Here's what doesn't change. None of the instruments is the point. The Word is at the center, and every sound in the room is there to carry it. The drum holds the time. The strings or the reeds hold the melody. The voice holds the words. And the sangat holds the listening. Every sound has a part.
screen: `THE HARMONIUM AND THE TABLA.` · `THE REBAB, SARANDA AND TAUS.` · `BRINGING THE STRINGS BACK.` · `EVERYTHING CARRIES THE WORD.` · then, large: `EVERY SOUND HAS A PART.`

segments.voice: Play a recording of kirtan if you can, or any music with a few instruments. Listen once, and pick out just the drum. Follow only that. Then let the drum go and find the melody: the harmonium, or the strings. Follow only that. Then find the voice. Finally, let them all come back together, and hear how each one leans on the others. If there's no music near you, do the same with the sounds of the room. The bell holds the time.
Instruments in the room. Harmonium and tabla today, rebab, saranda and taus from the Gurus' time, and every one of them there to carry the Word.
Your line: every sound has a part. Today, pick out one sound you usually tune out, a fridge, a bird, a voice, and give it your full attention. Day one hundred six.

107.title: The pause line
107.hook: rahao means pause; it marks the refrain that holds a hymn's center
107.howItsDone: In the Guru Granth Sahib, many shabads mark a central line with the word rahao; in kirtan that line is usually sung as the refrain, and in explaining a shabad teachers often begin from it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the instruments in the room: harmonium, tabla, and the old strings. Your line was every sound has a part. Did you give one ignored sound your full attention? Day one hundred seven.
screen: `INSTRUMENTS IN THE ROOM — EVERY SOUND HAS A PART.`

segments.voice: A friend is telling a long story. The details wander all over: who said what, where they parked, what the weather was like. Then, somewhere in the middle, there's one sentence where the voice changes. And I just realized, I don't want to live like that anymore. That's the story. Everything else is the setting around it. Good songs work the same way. The verses move around; the chorus comes back and tells you what it's all about. In the Guru Granth Sahib, many hymns have a line like that, and the Gurus marked it, right there on the page, with a single word.
screen: `THE SENTENCE WHERE THE VOICE CHANGES.` → `THE CHORUS COMES BACK.` → `ONE WORD MARKS IT.`

segments.voice: Rahao. It means pause, or stay, or dwell here. In the Guru Granth Sahib you'll find it written after a line or a couplet in many shabads, like a little flag. That line is the rahao line, and it holds the hymn's center. Here's the key that many Sikh teachers give for reading a shabad: find the rahao first. The other verses are often questions, pictures, examples, stories. The rahao line is the main thought they all circle around. Read it, and the rest of the hymn falls into place. It's the point of the friend's story. It's the thing to take home. And in kirtan you can hear it. When a shabad is sung, the rahao line usually becomes the refrain. The singers go out into a verse, and then they come back to the rahao, again and again. So the structure of the music matches the structure of the meaning. Every time the melody comes home, it comes home to the center. Notice that the word itself means pause. The Gurus didn't just put a label on it. They told you what to do there. Stop. Stay a while. Let this line sink in before you move on. Here is a scripture with a built-in instruction to slow down, right at the center of the hymn. You don't need to read Gurmukhi to use the idea. Translations of the Granth often keep the word rahao in place. Find it, and you've found the heart of the hymn.
screen: `RAHAO — PAUSE, STAY, DWELL.` · `FIND THE RAHAO FIRST.` · `THE REFRAIN IN KIRTAN.` · `A BUILT-IN INSTRUCTION TO SLOW DOWN.` · then, large: `PAUSE HERE.`

segments.voice: If you can, open any shabad from the Guru Granth Sahib, on a page, an app or a website with translations. Look for the word rahao. Read the line it marks, slowly, once or twice. Then close your eyes and stay with it. Don't go on to the rest of the hymn. Just pause there, the way the word asks. If you can't look one up right now, take the one sentence from your own week that mattered most, and pause with that. The bell holds the time.
Rahao. Pause, dwell here: the word that marks a hymn's central line, sung again and again as the refrain.
Your line: pause here. Today, when someone says the sentence that matters most, don't rush past it. Stop, and let it land. Day one hundred seven.

108.title: Listening with the words
108.hook: follow the Gurmukhi and its meaning as the hymn is sung
108.howItsDone: Many gurdwaras display the words of the shabad being sung on a screen, in Gurmukhi with transliteration and translation, and Sikhs at home often follow along using apps or printed gutkas.

segments.voice: Yesterday, rahao, the pause line at a hymn's center. Your line was pause here. Did you let one important sentence land? Day one hundred eight.

A film in a language you don't speak, with subtitles. At first the eyes race along the bottom of the screen and miss the faces. Then something shifts: the actor's voice breaks at the same moment the words go by, and the two lock together. Not reading, not listening, but both at once, and the scene hits twice as hard. In many gurdwaras today there's something similar. On a screen near the front, as the hymn is sung, the Gurmukhi words appear line by line, and under them, the sounds in English letters, and under that, a translation.
screen: `SUBTITLES THAT CLICK.` → `THE VOICE AND THE WORDS LOCK.` → `THE SCREEN NEAR THE FRONT.`

segments.voice: For four days you've practiced listening: just listening, then the mood of the raag, then the instruments, then the rahao line. Today adds the words. The practice is simple: as a shabad is sung, follow along with it. The Gurmukhi if you can read it, the sounds if you can't, and the meaning either way. Sound and sense together. Why bother? Because for Sikhs, the music is never just music. Guru Ram Das says it in the Guru Granth Sahib. In paraphrase: the Word is the Guru, and the Guru is the Word, and within the Word is all the nectar. The raag carries the mood; the words carry the teaching. When you hear both at once, the hymn can reach all of you. Here's what often happens the first time you try. You lose your place. The singer repeats a line you weren't expecting, or jumps back to the rahao, and your eyes are three lines behind. That's normal. Kirtan repeats on purpose. Let the rahao be your anchor: when you're lost, look for it, because the singers will come back to it. Some Sikhs who grew up outside Punjab say this is how they came to know the Granth. Not in a classroom, but on a Sunday morning, reading along with the screen, line by line, year after year, until one day a line in Gurmukhi meant something without the translation. And you don't need the gurdwara to do this. Apps and websites show the Gurmukhi, the sounds and a translation together, and many recordings are easy to follow along with.
screen: `FOUR DAYS OF LISTENING, THEN WORDS.` · `THE WORD IS THE GURU.` · `LOST? FIND THE RAHAO.` · `LINE BY LINE, YEAR AFTER YEAR.` · then, large: `SOUND AND SENSE TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: If you can, play one shabad and open its words beside it, in Gurmukhi, in English letters, and in translation. Follow along once. Let your eyes move with the voice. When you lose your place, don't stop the music. Look for the rahao line and wait for it to come back. If you can't play one right now, read a single line of a shabad aloud, slowly, then read its meaning, then say the line again. The bell holds the time.
Listening with the words. Following a shabad's Gurmukhi and its meaning while it's sung, so the sound and the sense arrive together.
Your line: sound and sense together. Today, read along once with one hymn or one song, and notice the moment the words and the music lock. Day one hundred eight.

109.title: Humming first
109.hook: hum quietly with a recording before trying the words
109.howItsDone: Many children in Sikh homes learn shabads by humming and singing along with recordings or with family, and kirtan teachers often have beginners learn a tune before its words.

segments.voice: Yesterday, listening with the words, following a shabad line by line. Your line was sound and sense together. Did the words and music lock, even once? Day one hundred nine.
screen: `LISTENING WITH THE WORDS — SOUND AND SENSE TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: When did you last sing out loud where someone could hear? For some adults it's happy birthday, sung badly, at the back of the group. Somewhere along the way, singing got handed over to people with good voices. And yet. Watch someone washing dishes alone, or a parent rocking a baby at two in the morning, or a person waiting at a crosswalk with earbuds in. Some of them are humming. No words, no audience, nobody judging. Humming is the singing people do before they remember to be embarrassed. That's exactly where kirtan starts.
screen: `WHEN DID YOU LAST SING ALOUD?` → `DISHES, A BABY, A CROSSWALK.` → `SINGING BEFORE EMBARRASSMENT.`

segments.voice: Five days of listening. Now five days of singing, and the first one doesn't use words at all. Humming first. Some kirtan teachers start a nervous beginner this way, and children in Sikh homes can pick up a shabad's tune before they can read it. You put on a recording, and you hum along under it, quietly, following the tune. Why start there? Three reasons. First, the melody. A shabad's tune can wander, following its raag, and it's hard to learn the notes and the words at the same time. Humming lets you learn the road before you carry anything down it. Second, the fear. Humming is almost impossible to do badly. Nobody's listening for your pronunciation. Your voice gets used to joining in, without the pressure of getting it right. Third, the body. When you hum, you can feel it in your chest and face. The music stops being something outside you and becomes something happening inside you. That matters, because Sikhs say kirtan isn't a performance for an audience. In the Japji, Guru Nanak says, in paraphrase: sing, and listen, and keep love in your mind, and sorrow will leave, and peace will come home. Notice: sing and listen, together. Not sing well. Nobody is grading a hum. Kirtan in the gurdwara is often led by trained musicians called ragis, but the sangat joins in too. The Gurus' hymns are meant to be in ordinary mouths. Yours included. Start with a hum.
screen: `FIVE DAYS OF SINGING BEGIN.` · `LEARN THE ROAD FIRST.` · `A HUM CAN'T BE WRONG.` · `SING, LISTEN, KEEP LOVE IN MIND.` · then, large: `HUM FIRST.`

segments.voice: Put on a shabad you heard this week, or any gentle tune you know. Sit comfortably. Close your mouth and breathe through your nose. Now hum along with it, very softly, just under the recording. Don't worry about the right notes. Feel the buzz in your lips, your chest, the bones of your face. If you lose the tune, just listen until you find it again, then join back in. Keep humming, softly, all the way through. The bell holds the time.
Humming first. Joining a shabad's melody without words, so the tune, and your voice, get ready before the words arrive.
Your line: hum first. Today, hum one tune while you do something ordinary: the dishes, the walk, the wait. Day one hundred nine.

110.title: Singing Waheguru
110.hook: the simplest kirtan is singing Waheguru to a simple tune
110.howItsDone: Sikh congregations often sing Waheguru simran together, a single word repeated to a simple tune, and many Sikhs repeat Waheguru through the day, sung, spoken or silently.

segments.voice: Yesterday, humming first, the tune before the words. Your line was hum first. Did you catch yourself humming over the dishes or on a walk? Day one hundred ten.

Go back to the second day of this whole path. The word was Waheguru, and the line was just: wow. Wonder, plus teacher. The wonderful Guru. You've probably heard it many times since. Now picture the end of a long evening program at a gurdwara. The shabads are done. The harmonium player starts a slow, simple tune, four or five notes going round, and the whole room begins to sing one word. Waheguru. Waheguru. Grandparents, teenagers, tired kids leaning on their parents. Nobody needs a screen for this. Nobody needs to read Gurmukhi. Everyone knows the words, because there's only one.
screen: `DAY TWO: WAHEGURU. WOW.` → `A SLOW TUNE GOING ROUND.` → `EVERYONE KNOWS THE ONE WORD.`

segments.voice: Singing Waheguru is the simplest kirtan there is. One word, one tune, sung again and again. Sikhs often call it Waheguru simran: remembering God by singing the name. Waheguru has a special place in Sikh life. Sikhs call it the gurmantar, the Guru's own word to repeat. The early Sikh poet Bhai Gurdas wrote of Waheguru as that word, the gurmantar. And in the Guru Granth Sahib itself, near the end, poets at the Gurus' court, known as the Bhatts, sing the word over and over in praise of the Guru. It's what Sikhs say when they greet each other in the Khalsa way, what they whisper when they wake, what they say when they're amazed or afraid. And singing it does something that saying it doesn't. The tune slows the word down. Wah, the wonder, gets to open all the way. Guru, the teacher who leads from dark to light, lands softly at the end. The repeating stops being boring and starts being steady, like waves. After a few rounds, you're not thinking about the word. You're inside it. That's the point of simran: not to think about God, but to remember, with the whole self. There's no one correct tune. Every gurdwara, every family, seems to have its own. Some are slow and low, almost a lullaby. Some pick up speed until the whole room is swaying. The tune serves the name. If you only ever learn one piece of kirtan, many Sikhs would say, let it be this. It fits in any voice, any room, any day.
screen: `ONE WORD, ONE TUNE.` · `THE GURMANTAR.` · `THE TUNE SLOWS THE WORD DOWN.` · `NOT THINKING, REMEMBERING.` · then, large: `THE NAME, SUNG.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. Take one breath. Now, softly, sing Waheguru five times. Any simple tune: two or three notes is plenty. Or use the hum from yesterday and just put the word into it. Wah, then Guru. Let the wah open like a surprise, and the Guru settle. If singing feels like too much, hum it, or whisper it. After the fifth, stay quiet and listen to the room. If you'd like, sing it five times more. The bell holds the time.
Singing Waheguru. The simplest kirtan: the gurmantar, the wonderful Guru, sung again and again to a simple tune.
Your line: the name, sung. Today, sing Waheguru five times somewhere unexpected: the car, the shower, the stairs. Day one hundred ten.

111.title: One line
111.hook: learn one short refrain and sing only that
111.howItsDone: Many Sikhs carry a favorite line of gurbani, a tuk, that they sing or repeat through the day, and kirtan teachers often start beginners with a single refrain.

segments.voice: Yesterday, singing Waheguru, one word to a simple tune. Your line was the name, sung. Did you sing it somewhere unexpected? Day one hundred eleven.

A single line of a song can live in a head for years. A lullaby a grandmother sang, a hymn from school, the chorus of a song from a hard summer. The verses are long gone, or were never learned. But that one line comes back, uninvited, in the shower, on a long drive, in a hospital waiting room. It has been doing quiet work all along. Nobody needed the whole song. The line was enough. Yesterday you sang one word. Today, one line: a single short refrain from the Guru's hymns, learned well enough to carry around.
screen: `THE LINE THAT LIVES IN YOUR HEAD.` → `IT COMES BACK UNINVITED.` → `ONE SHORT REFRAIN.`

segments.voice: Here's a gentle rule some kirtan teachers give beginners: don't try to learn a whole shabad. Learn one line. Sing only that, again and again, until it's yours. Which line? There are a few good places to look. The rahao line, from day one hundred seven, is the heart of a hymn and is already built to be repeated. Or the opening of the Mool Mantar you met on days four and five: Ik Onkar, Satnam. Or a short line from any shabad that caught you this week. Why is one line enough? Because of what the Gurus say a single teaching can do. In the Japji, Guru Nanak says, in paraphrase, that within the mind are gems, jewels and rubies, if you listen to even one teaching of the Guru. Even one. The Gurus weren't asking people to memorize a library. They were trusting that one true line, really taken in, can open the rest. And a sung line goes deeper than a read one. You've learned it with your breath and your ear and your voice, not just your eyes. That's why it comes back uninvited, at the right moments, the way that old song does. Some Sikhs talk about a line of gurbani, a tuk, staying with them through a hard year, or rising up at a funeral, or at a wedding. Nobody planned it. The line had been waiting. So today, pick one. Keep it short. Sing it until you don't need to look.

segments.voice: Choose your line. If you're not sure, take Ik Onkar, Satnam. Say it once, slowly, to be sure of the sounds. Now sing it, softly, on two or three notes, or on the Waheguru tune from yesterday. Sing it again. And again. Let it get easier each time. Don't reach for a second line. Just this one, until it's as familiar as your own name. The bell holds the time.
One line. A single short refrain of gurbani, a tuk, sung until it's yours, trusted to do its quiet work.
Your line: one line is enough. Today, sing your one line three times, morning, midday and night. Day one hundred eleven.

112.title: Singing back
112.hook: in the gurdwara the sangat sings the refrain back to the singers
112.howItsDone: In many gurdwaras the ragis lead kirtan while the sangat listens, and at many programs, and in some kirtan traditions, the congregation sings lines back to the singers together.

segments.voice: Yesterday, one line of gurbani, sung until it's yours. Your line was one line is enough. Did your line come back to you at a strange moment? Day one hundred twelve.

In a stadium, one section starts a song, and it rolls around the stands until thousands of strangers are singing the same words. Nobody sounds good alone. Together, it's enormous. Or something smaller: a birthday table where everyone's slightly off key and it's still the best part of the night. Something happens when voices join that doesn't happen to any voice alone. Now a gurdwara in the evening. The ragis at the front sing a line of a shabad. They pause. And the whole room sings the line back to them. They sing the next. The room answers again.
screen: `A STADIUM OF STRANGERS SINGING.` → `THE BIRTHDAY TABLE, OFF KEY.` → `THE ROOM SINGS IT BACK.`

segments.voice: Sangat. You met the word on day thirteen: the congregation, the company you keep. Today you hear it. In many gurdwaras, especially at evening programs and in some styles of kirtan, the singers lead a line and the sangat sings it back. Call and answer. A child's voice next to a grandfather's, a beginner next to someone who's known the shabad for a lifetime, all on the same line. Nobody is performing. Everybody is part of it. Sikhs set great store by this. The Gurus taught that the company you keep shapes the person you become, and that the true sangat has a mark you can recognize. Guru Nanak asks in the Guru Granth Sahib, in paraphrase: how is the true congregation known? And he answers: it's where the one Name is spoken. Not a building. Not a membership. A gathering where people are remembering God together. That's why singing back matters. When you sing alone, you can drift, lose the tune, forget the words, get self-conscious. In the sangat, the voices around you carry you. When you falter, someone else has the line. When they falter, you do. And the singing does to the room what seva does in the kitchen: it dissolves the hierarchy for a while. This week you listened for instruments, found the rahao, read along, hummed, sang Waheguru, learned one line. Every one of those was practice for this moment: your voice, taking its place among the others. You don't have to sing well. You just have to sing with.
screen: `SANGAT — THE COMPANY YOU KEEP.` · `THE RAGIS LEAD, THE ROOM ANSWERS.` · `WHERE THE ONE NAME IS SPOKEN.` · `THE OTHERS CARRY YOU.` · then, large: `VOICES TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: If you can, play a recording of kirtan where the sangat sings back; many gurdwara recordings and live streams have it. When the singers lead a line, sing it back with the room, even quietly. If you can't find one, play any song you know and sing along once, all the way through, with the voices on the recording. Notice how much easier it is to sing when you're not alone. The bell holds the time.
Sangat. The congregation, singing back, voice with voice. Your week: instruments, rahao, reading along, humming, Waheguru, one line, and the sangat.
Your line: voices together. Today, sing along once with other voices, a recording, a room, a car full of friends, and let them carry you. Day one hundred twelve.
